abstract: Alternative splicing diversifies the transcriptome and shapes cell fate across development, tissue function, and disease. Single-cell RNA sequencing can link isoforms to cell states, but these methods often lack the throughput and coverage to accurately call splice variants. As a result, rare isoforms are often missed, especially in underrepresented cell types. Here, we present Catch*ReSeq, a targeted enrichment method that yields isoform-resolved readouts linked to host transcriptomes from standard single-cell libraries for the capture of rare isoforms. We found more oligo(dT)-primer cDNA originating from internal A-rich sequences than from terminal polyA tails (80-fold enrichment for simian immunodeficiency virus (SIV) and over 6-fold for host transcripts), fracturing cDNA and obscuring isoforms. Catch*ReSeq exploits this fracture to infer each molecule's isoform of origin. In SIV-infected macaque CD4+ T cells, Catch*ReSeq detected up to 13 times as many infected cells as standard 10X and resolved spliced viral isoforms that 10X missed entirely. Splice+ cells carried a translational host program independent of how much virus they transcribed, a distinction invisible to standard single-cell sequencing methods. From macaque and PWH on ART, Catch*ReSeq recovered 13-fold more virus-transcribing cells than 10X, including splice+ cells. We also demonstrated the generalizability of Catch*ReSeq across biological systems by applying it in combination with lineage barcoding to probe alternative splicing in clonally expanded CD4+ T cells, and separately in mouse liver regeneration. As Catch*ReSeq works with archived cDNA and can be redesigned for new targets after the fact, it allows rare isoform profiling on existing biobanked and clinical samples.
